Report positive and negative requests. Omit the defective refusal multiple-choice item with no valid option; wider reporting is extension only.
In pairs, one learner asks a partner to bring a notebook or not to move a bag. A third learner reports the request orally. Speaking has no platform score.
Rehearse request reporting in a constrained recognition task; wider tense/question transformations are optional.
Compare reporting-verb complements; never mark said to us that as inherently ungrammatical.
Teach adjective/adverb function rather than an absolute word-position rule.
Teach experiencer versus cause; a person can be interesting.
Use too/enough, count/mass quantifiers and the taught positions.
Compare actions and use intensifiers with supplied contexts; omit gender generalisations.
Categorise ending functions in examples. Reuse adjective category; -ly, not the whole -ively string, is the adverb-forming ending in actively.
Read the history adaptation, then optionally write a three-sentence summary in time order. Summary is an extension, not the required style-description writing outcome.
Read style/fashion distinctions with a supplied example. Optional personal response is unscored.

With the printed book, match idioms to meanings: last word in fashion → latest fashion; lose one’s temper → become angry; sit on the phone → spend a long time on the phone; get out of bed on the wrong side → be in a bad mood; put on airs → act as if more important than others. Use textbook and Armenian designer source cards; no ranking, celebrity recall or purchases required.
Use supplied information for a short class presentation or discussion if desired. Oral performance stays classroom-assessed and outside platform denominators.
Identify complete pro/con/neutral statements; do not score agreement about uniforms.
Recognise a preference with a reason. Practise polite disagreement orally or in an unscored planning note.
Read the practice model, plan the independent picnic note, then use the class-photo task only after content/rubric/workload acceptance. One reviewed note covers two linked writing outcomes.

Use the original Bidstrup picture sequence in the learner’s book, in its printed order. Describe what each panel visibly shows, then write a short story. No image is republished; obtain image permission before any future platform use. Not a substitute for activity 25.

Use the printed song only in an authorised classroom setting; invite learners to identify repeated words or discuss its message. No platform song playback, lyric upload, singing mark or core fashion-listening credit.
Read or listen to the printed poem under the school’s permissions and discuss one image or repeated idea. No platform recording or core listening credit.
Review a/an/the/zero in neutral, self-contained clothing contexts. Replace the printed factual errors and stereotypes.
Review comparisons with explicit groups and supplied information, not geographical trivia.

guides.title: Describe without judging
guides.text: A word can describe behaviour, such as patient, or appearance, such as curly-haired. Neither appearance nor a clothing style tells us everything about a person. Choose a word from the evidence in the sentence, not from a stereotype.
guides.workedExample: Someone who says “please” and thanks a helper is being polite.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Build and use words
guides.text: A verb and its noun can have different endings and spellings. Read the sentence to decide which word class is needed, then use a learned form. Do not invent a suffix. Behaviour and behavior are British and American spellings of the same noun.
guides.workedExample: educate → education: Education helps people learn.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Style words
guides.text: Casual means relaxed and informal; classic describes an established lasting style; retro is inspired by the past; trendy is popular now; chic means elegant and stylish; flashy is very noticeable. Conservative suggests traditional choices; eccentric suggests unusual choices; sloppy means not neat; old-fashioned means no longer modern. These labels describe a look and are not judgments about a person’s worth.
guides.workedExample: A look inspired by clothes from an earlier decade can be called retro.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Report a request
guides.text: Use asked or told + person + to + base verb for a positive request or instruction. The taught negative pattern is asked/told + person + not to + base verb. Keep the original meaning. Wider statements and reported questions are optional textbook extensions.
guides.workedExample: “Please close the door,” she said to Aram. → She asked Aram to close the door.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Describe a thing, an action or a feeling
guides.text: An adjective can describe a noun after a linking verb: The tea smells pleasant. An adverb can describe how an action happens: She answered politely. With the taught feeling pairs, -ed commonly describes the person experiencing a feeling and -ing describes its cause. A person can also be the cause.
guides.workedExample: An exciting story makes a reader excited.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Enough, too and comparisons
guides.text: Enough shows sufficiency: enough time; warm enough. Too shows excess for a stated purpose: too cold to sit outside. Use too many with countable plurals and too much with an amount. Compare two things or actions with a comparative; use a superlative for the extreme in a stated group. Much and far can strengthen a comparative.
guides.workedExample: The room is warm enough to work in. This route is much shorter than that one.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Read for evidence
guides.text: First identify the whole topic. Then reread for the detail or time marker a question asks about. A supplied card is enough: do not guess from outside knowledge. A statement can go beyond the text even if it sounds plausible. Identify the writer’s opinion without treating it as the only acceptable opinion.
guides.workedExample: If a text says “some people”, it does not establish “everyone”.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Plan a note for a reader
guides.text: Read the incoming message. Plan a greeting, your style and clothing details, reasons, and a polite response to the suggestion. Check that the reader can follow your ideas. Use your own or an invented preference. Review the rubric and count the words; do not add irrelevant sentences just to reach a number.
guides.workedExample: I see why you like that idea. I would choose a different colour because it goes with my jacket.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

guides.title: Choose an article from the context
guides.text: Use a or an for a newly introduced, unspecified singular countable noun. Choose by the next sound: a hat, an apple. Use the when the reader can identify the particular thing. General plural nouns and unspecified amounts can have no article. In these tasks type zero explicitly; an empty field means no answer.
guides.workedExample: I found a hat. The hat was on a chair. Hats can protect us from the sun.
guides.capacity: Teaching support; contributes no independent assessment capacity.

sourceSets.title: Clothing through time
sourceSets.text:
Clothing has changed over time. In ancient societies such as Egypt, Greece and Rome, clothes could show a person’s social position.

During the Industrial Revolution, new manufacturing methods made clothing more widely available. This changed how clothes were produced and bought.

Today, clothes can still express personal choices and cultural traditions. Some designers also think about reducing waste and the environmental effects of making clothes. The history of clothing includes changes in materials, production and people’s choices.
sourceSets.adaptation: Shortened from the textbook; removes sweeping claims about all people or periods. All questions rely only on this supplied text.

sourceSets.title: Fashion and personal style
sourceSets.text:
Fashion describes trends that are popular at a particular time. Personal style is the way someone chooses to dress. A person may use a trend, adapt it or decide not to follow it.

Ani notices that bright jackets are popular this month. She keeps wearing her plain shirt because it is comfortable and she likes combining it with different trousers. This is one example of a personal choice.

Classic styles use simple designs that remain popular for a long time. Retro styles draw on clothes from an earlier period. Casual clothes are relaxed choices for everyday activities. These labels describe clothing, not the whole person wearing it. An outfit alone cannot tell us someone’s character.
sourceSets.adaptation: Original simplified adaptation of the book’s distinctions with an authored example. Avoids universal claims, gender rules and judgments about a learner’s clothing.

sourceSets.title: Two sources about design
sourceSets.text:
Card A — textbook
The textbook describes Coco Chanel as a designer associated with simpler, comfortable clothes. This card gives one example of how a designer can influence clothing.

Card B — Armenian design
Aram Nikolyan is an Armenian designer. His studio is called NIKOLYAN. The Fashion and Design Chamber of Armenia describes his work as drawing on Armenian culture and traditions while creating contemporary clothing. Here, contemporary means belonging to the present time.

Read the cards for information. You do not need to prefer either designer or buy any of their clothes.
sourceSets.adaptation: Card A paraphrases the provided textbook; Card B paraphrases the FDC profile. No dates, rankings, purchases or prior designer knowledge are assessed.

definition.prompt:
Your new classmate Sona writes:
“Hi! We are choosing clothes for our class photo. I am thinking of a bright jacket. What kind of clothes do you like wearing? Would you choose something bright too?”

Write Sona an 80–100-word note. Describe your preferred style and give at least two clothing details. Explain your choices with reasons. Reply politely to Sona’s suggestion: you may agree, suggest another choice or combine the ideas. You may invent a preference. Do not include private personal information or send the note to anyone. Your choice of style is not graded.

assistance.policy: No model answer or translation during the proposed reviewed submission. Record actual support; teacher-returned revisions retain their history. External assistance cannot be guaranteed absent.

criteria.label: Task and audience
descriptors: No relevant assessable response to the task.
Partly describes a preference; important details, reasons or the reply to the classmate are missing.
Main purpose and audience are clear, with a minor omission or a length deviation that limits detail.
Describes a style with relevant details and reasons, and responds politely to the classmate’s suggestion within the intended brief.

criteria.label: Organisation
descriptors: Ideas are mainly disconnected; the reader must reconstruct the message.
The note is generally easy to follow, with occasional abrupt links or repetition.
Ideas form a coherent note with a clear order and suitable basic links.

criteria.label: Vocabulary
descriptors: Insufficient meaningful vocabulary to communicate the task.
Limited or inaccurate word choices often make meaning unclear.
Vocabulary is generally adequate; occasional inappropriate choices do not obscure the main message.
Suitable clothing and style words express the intended ideas clearly.

criteria.label: Grammar and written clarity
descriptors: The intended message is too unclear to assess this criterion.
Frequent errors obscure parts of the message.
Meaning remains generally clear despite recurring grammar, spelling or punctuation errors.
Taught structures communicate clearly; occasional errors do not obstruct meaning.

assessmentNotes: One submitted note supplies one linked observation of description and written interaction, not two independent samples.
Criterion levels 0–3 are proposed, total 0–12. No pass threshold is set.
Length is guidance and a review flag, never an automatic zero or overall failure. A strong response is not capped solely for a small word-count deviation.
Draft, missing, pending and technically failed work are states, not rubric marks.
Do not score wealth, style preference, agreement, body shape, personality or personal disclosure.
A returned revision is a continuation of the same observed task, not an independent baseline.

practice.prompt: A classmate writes: “Our reading club is having a picnic. I thought of wearing a shirt and formal trousers. What would you wear, and why? Would you suggest anything different?” Write an 80–100-word reply with two clothing details, reasons and a polite response. You may invent your preference. Use the planning guide and rubric, then revise your note.
practice.comparison: Same description/audience/reason procedure as W01, with a different supplied occasion. Neither task is claimed as unseen or as new independent reasoning. Review before any future assessment allocation.

model.incoming: A friend asks what you would wear for a walk in the park and suggests a thick coat.
model.text:
Hi Ada,
For a walk in the park, I would choose a casual style. I would wear comfortable trousers, a cotton top and trainers because I want to move easily. I like plain clothes, but I sometimes add a colourful scarf. Your idea of a thick coat could be useful on a cold day. If the weather is warm, I would prefer a light jacket that I can carry in my bag. We can choose different clothes and still enjoy our walk together.
See you soon,
Nare
annotation: The greeting and reply address a reader.
The note describes clothes and explains choices.
The response considers the friend’s suggestion politely; it need not agree completely.
This is one possible practice model, not a template whose opinions or phrases must be copied.
model.releaseRule: Practice support only; do not show alongside W01 during a reviewed submission. Shared procedure and topic are recorded as familiar.

workloadProposal.learnerMinutes: 20–25 for planning, writing and self-check after practice; estimate to pilot, not a timed limit
workloadProposal.teacherMinutes: 4–6 per initial submission; 120–180 minutes for 30 learners, plus any return/review time. Estimate awaiting a workload decision.
workloadProposal.cadence: One reviewed note for this unit, with a returned revision if needed. Do not create separate scored S13 and S14 submissions by default.
workloadProposal.baseline: Keep the automatic diagnostic before practice. Writing baseline is proposed as separately tracked and non-gating, but not enabled by this packet.
teacherChecklist: Read the note for meaning before assigning levels.
Assess each criterion independently; quote a short relevant feature in feedback.
Return technically incomplete work for revision where appropriate rather than manufacturing four zeros.
Give one clear strength and one next step; retain the reviewed submission version.
